title: From One Smart Bot to a Kitchen Crew
subtitle: How Google ADK turns prototypes into production multi-agent systems
intro: Your single AI assistant answered 40,000 requests yesterday. Each time it tried to do everything alone — and slowed down.
takeaway: ADK lets you split work across specialized agents with predictable graph paths, but you must manage context or the crew stalls.

sections.heading: The analogy: a restaurant kitchen crew
sections.body: Imagine one chef doing everything versus a kitchen crew. One chef takes orders, cooks, and serves — slow and messy. A crew splits jobs: one greets, one cooks, one checks quality. An agent is an AI helper with one job and tools. Orchestration is the head chef deciding who acts next. Powerful, but only if organized — which is the next puzzle.

sections.heading: Why does this exist? From prototypes to production
sections.body: That is why Google's ADK exists. ADK is an open-source Agent Development Kit for production agents, not prototypes. It weaves deterministic code — fixed rules like 'always check ID' — with LLM reasoning, flexible AI thinking. Work is a graph: explicit paths like A -> B -> C for predictable outcomes. It works in Python, TypeScript, Go, Java, Kotlin and scales to enterprise services. More agents, more to manage.

sections.heading: What can go wrong? When your crew gets confused
sections.body: What breaks if usage grows 100x? Context. Context is each agent's short-term memory of the conversation. If every agent saves everything, memory bloats, costs spike, and agents use stale info. Even with graphs, a loop or missed handoff can stall the system. ADK lets you test, evaluate, and debug paths before deploy, so handoffs stay predictable, not just smart.

steps.narration: User request arrives and needs multiple skills.
Orchestrator decides which agent acts next.
Specialist Agent A handles its job with tools.
Specialist Agent B handles the next job.
Graph defines explicit A -> B -> C path for predictability.
Shared context passes only needed memory between agents.

quiz.q: What is orchestration in a multi-agent system?
options: The head-chef logic deciding which agent acts next
quiz.why: Orchestration is coordinating who does what and when, not just having smarter models.

quiz.q: What fails first if usage grows 100x?
options: Context/memory bloat leading to cost and stale info
quiz.why: If every agent keeps everything, context bloats, costs spike, and handoffs use stale info.

quiz.q: Why weave deterministic code with LLM reasoning?
options: To combine predictable rules with flexible thinking
quiz.why: ADK's idea is reliable logic plus adaptive reasoning for predictable yet intelligent outcomes.

extra: ADK 2.0 adds Agents CLI to scaffold, test, and deploy agents from your IDE.
